extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, script adapters, and filmmakers (writers adapting novels/plays to film)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for adapting novels/plays to film: selecting suitable source material, immersing in its spirit, reducing events to filmable actions, reinventing for filmic rhythms, and designing character and cast for screen storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose sources with conflict distributed on all three levels
rubrics_metrics.description: If you must adapt, come down a rung or two from 'pure' literature and look for stories in which conflict is distributed on all three levels . . . with an emphasis at the extra-personal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer social novels (extra-personal/camera-attractive conflicts) over dense modernist works (no Proust, no Joyce, no Kafka). Example: Pierre Boulle’s The Bridge on the River Kwai (good for film); avoid works whose genius is primarily internal and literary, which often do not translate to screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immerse yourself in the original before planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the work over and over without taking notes until you feel infused with its spirit. Do not make choices or plan moves until you’ve rubbed shoulders with its society, read their faces, smelled their cologne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieve a 'godlike knowledge' of the world; never assume the original writer did all homework. Only after full immersion should you begin outlining or cutting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce each event to a one- or two-sentence statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce each event to a one- or two-sentence statement of what happens and no more. No psychology, no sociology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize events in plain dramatic actions (e.g., 'He walks into the house expecting a confrontation with his wife, but discovers a note telling him she’s left him for another man'). This yields a clear basis for a step-outline and prevents overreliance on internal exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to reinvent
rubrics_metrics.description: The second principle of adaptation: Be willing to reinvent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novel is not well-told for film or is too long, treat your task as reinvention rather than literal adaptation. Expect to cut, reorder, and create new scenes to fit the rhythms and needs of cinema; accept critics saying 'the film’s not like the novel' if the film is true to its medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the story in filmic rhythms and turn the mental into the physical
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the story in filmic rhythms while keeping the spirit of the original. Turn what is mental into the physical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reorder events chronologically (from first to last) to create a step-outline, cut or add scenes where necessary, and find visual expressions for inner conflicts rather than relying on self-explanatory dialogue or interior monologue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize medium-appropriate design over slavish fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek a design that expresses the spirit of the original yet stays within the rhythms of a film, ignoring the risk that critics may say, 'But the film’s not like the novel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reinvention produces an excellent film even when radically deviating from the original, critics will accept it; conversely, do not 'butcher' a beloved original without producing an equal or better work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study exemplars of successful adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: To learn adaptation study the work of successful adapters (e.g., Ruth Prawer Jhabvala).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare step-outlines and scene-by-scene changes between novel and screenplay to learn techniques; note that successful adapters often choose source authors whose conflicts suit film (Forster, Henry James, Jean Rhys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with images of social/environmental conflict and lead to inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: The challenge is to start with images of social/environmental conflict and lead us into the complexities of personal relationships, to begin on the surface of what’s said and done and guide us to a perception of the inner life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the camera’s natural expressivity (extra-personal) to move the audience from observable action into implied inner meaning; 'Show, don’t tell' is the ultimate creative task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid melodrama by matching motivation to action
rubrics_metrics.description: Melodrama is not the result of overexpression, but of under-motivation; we feel a scene is melodramatic if we cannot believe that motivation matches action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the power of an event is supported by the sum total of its causes—fully lift the forces that drive characters so audience accepts extreme actions. Writing 'big scenes' is acceptable if thoroughly motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle logical 'holes' responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'hole' is a missing link in the chain of cause and effect; holes reduce credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, close the hole by forging a link (even if it means adding a scene). If that creates awkwardness, decide whether the audience will notice; either hide it by pacing or expose the hole and deny it (admit the gap transparently within the story). Use resolution scenes when necessary to prevent audiences from being swallowed by inconsistency (example: THE TERMINATOR's resolution scene).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design the inciting incident to fit the character (Mind Worm concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like the 'Mind Worm' conceit, create an event geared to the unique nature of the character—the precise happening needed to send him on a quest that reaches the limits of his being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore the character’s inscape to design an Inciting Incident that reveals and tests core traits; the event should be bespoke to that protagonist (e.g., finding or losing a fortune).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization vs. True Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization is the sum of observable qualities (appearance, mannerisms, occupation, etc.). True Character waits behind this mask—who the person is at heart (loyal vs. disloyal, honest vs. liar, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design both layers: use characterization as clues but reveal True Character through choices under pressure (dilemmas). True Character is best expressed through decisive actions in conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make desire central and explicit (multiple temporal scopes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to True Character is desire. Ask: What does this character want? Now? Soon? Overall? Knowingly? Unknowingly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define conscious and unconscious desires across time horizons; clear answers give command of the role and inform motivation and action in scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing characters to mono-explanations or case studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce characters to case studies or mono-explanations (e.g., 'an episode of child abuse' as sole cause); avoid nailing motivation to a single, overspecified cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think through to a solid understanding of motive but leave some mystery and irrationality so the audience can use its own experience to enrich the character; overly specific causes can diminish a character's universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show character through action and subtext, not self-explanatory dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: What a character says about himself may or may not be true; self-explanatory dialogue meant to convince us is boring and phony unless validated in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the audience confirm or contradict a character’s self-claims via behavior under pressure. Use subtext rather than explicit self-analysis. Example: Rick's line in CASABLANCA is validated later by action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create dimension via contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimension means contradiction: either within deep character (guilt-ridden ambition) or between characterization and deep character (a charming thief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build consistent contradictions that produce complexity (e.g., Macbeth’s ambition vs. guilt). Avoid one-off inconsistent actions that break credibility (don't have a character nice throughout then randomly kick a cat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the protagonist the most dimensional character
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist must be the most dimensional character in the cast to focus empathy on the star role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an antagonist or supporting character out-dimensions the protagonist, the Center of Good decentsers and the audience's emotional focus drifts (example: BLADE RUNNER). Keep the protagonist emotionally dominant to anchor the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design supporting cast to delineate protagonist's dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: All other characters exist primarily because of the relationship they strike to the protagonist and how each helps delineate the protagonist’s dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create supporting characters who provoke different aspects of the protagonist (e.g., one brings out sadness, another wit, another courage). Tertiary and bit parts should serve the protagonist—bit parts deliberately flat but with a fresh trait; avoid creating false anticipation by making bit parts overly interesting unless they reappear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic character: assign a blind obsession (humour)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic character is marked by a blind obsession—an attitude or fixation the character does not see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find the mania/humour that the comic character lacks awareness of; comedy depends on the character’s blindness. If the character recognizes the obsession, the comedy usually ends (example: Archie Bunker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave room for the actor; avoid over-directing behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave room for the actor: do not overwrite and pepper the page with constant description of behaviors, nuances of gesture, tones of voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell actors what they want, why, how they pursue it, what stops them, and the consequences—allow the actor to create subtext and behavior. Avoid excessive stage directions; imagine ideal casting while writing to remind yourself how little superb actors need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love all your characters (including villains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fall in love with all your characters. Embrace every role, even the bad people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers who love their characters find rich, surprising moments (e.g., sympathetic traits in villains). Portray antagonists as people solving their problems—avoid caricature and allow nuanced, believable behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build characters from observation and self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is self-knowledge: observation provides characterization; deeper understanding of deep character comes from self-knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect observed traits but assemble characters from parts (mix traits from different people and your self-knowledge). The more you know yourself, the better you can imagine truthful choices for others; borrow bits of humanity and combine them into cohesive, dimensional characters.
